newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Report finds widespread BSE failures in EU.
newsitem.headline: Report finds widespread BSE failures in EU.

text.p: A report by the European Commission found that many EU countries failed to enforce controls to prevent the spread of mad cow disease and protect public health, a Commission spokesman said on Saturday.

The unpublished report, presented this week to the EU's standing veterinary committee, was ordered by EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler after farm ministers rejected wider measures to fight the fatal disease, also known as bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE).
"The general conclusion is that more could be done by member states," Commission agriculture spokesman Gerard Kiely said.
One serious shortcoming was inadequate controls to prevent BSE-infected meat and bone meal being fed to cattle, he noted.
Another weakness in many member states was in the detection and diagnosis of BSE.
Kiely said the report was a summary of what was found during EU inspections in member states.
"We will follow up with specific national reports which will be discussed with member states to rectify mistakes," he said.
Fischler was furious that EU farm ministers threw out a proposal in December to ban from the human food chain offal from sheep and goats that can harbour scrapie or BSE.
Scrapie is a similar brain-wasting disease to BSE that has affected sheep for centuries.
Only France, Britain, Ireland, Sweden and Luxembourg supported the measure.
Others argued that the measure was unnecessary and too costly, claiming that their countries were free of BSE and scrapie.
The British government has claimed that BSE has been under-reported in continental Europe and this has been supported by a senior European Commission veterinary official.

Lars Hoelgaard recently told a European Parliament inquiry into BSE that some 57,000 animals were legally exported from Britain before such exports were banned in 1989 and before a ban on the use of suspect meat and bone meal in cattle feed.
About 1,600 BSE cases would have been expected from the 57,000 animals, he said.

But slightly less than 300 cases have been reported. Two-thirds of these cases were in Ireland and most of the rest in Portugal and France. Around 165,000 cases have been confirmed in Britain since the first outbreak in 1986.
The EU slapped a worldwide ban on British beef exports in March 1996 after London said BSE could possibly be transmitted to humans who ate infected beef.
